name: Coalition for Rainforest Nations (charityevals)
summary: The Coalition for Rainforest Nations helps rainforest countries in the UN climate talks, trains their teams to measure and report their forest results so they can be paid for cutting deforestation, and helps them sell forest carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. We model all of its 2024 programme spending ($4.0 million) in three branches: the forest kept by donors' results-based payments; the forest kept by credit sales, less the extra emissions of buyers who count the credits against their own targets; and the climate-finance goal agreed at COP29, valued as aid. Nearly all of the result is the finance goal, through a small judged share of the credit for a very large sum: CfRN's part of everyone's work on the goal, and how much of the goal's money is new and delivered, are the biggest uncertainties. The forest branches rest on one evaluation, Norway's payments to Guyana, credit CfRN with its share of all the money behind the forest kept (a sixth to a third of a percent), and are small; the credit sales are a small net harm at the best guesses. Every branch takes the missing-data discount.

sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: Everything the Coalition for Rainforest Nations (CfRN) spent on its one reported programme in 2024, the latest year filed: REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation), its "ongoing flagship program" (Part III). The return says the statements were not audited or reviewed by an accountant (Part XII line 2), so the Form 990 is the accounts. Its 2024 Annual Impact Statement describes three pillars inside that programme: the UN climate negotiations, national implementation (carbon-market laws, registries and sales) and data collection and capacity building. All three are modelled below, as three branches: forest kept by donors' results-based payments, forest kept by credit sales under Article 6 net of buyers' extra emissions, and the climate-finance goal (rbf_share_of_programme, fin_share_of_programme).

rows.label: Total expenses, calendar year 2024

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations Secretariat (EIN 26-3221530), Form 990 for calendar year 2024, IRS e-file XML (in the IRS's 2025 batch 11B)

rows.explainer: Programmes $4,048,414, management $803,008 and fundraising $23,926.

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programme

Salaries, benefits and payroll taxes, 2024

rows.explainer: Officers' pay $427,139, other salaries $722,918, benefits $241,477 and payroll taxes $133,542.

rows.label: Fees to forestry experts, 2024

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations Secretariat (EIN 26-3221530), Form 990 for calendar year 2024, IRS e-file XML (in the IRS's 2025 batch 11B)

rows.explainer: Contractors who train government forestry teams as staff would (Convention 1 counts them with staff). The other professional fees ($1,336,316: legal, registry and communications work) are left out: firms paid market rates, with no forgone pay.

rows.label: Share of the programme on measuring forest results for results-based payments
rows.explainer: CfRN reports no split of its one programme. Our judgment: 45% (30-60%) goes to work that lets rainforest countries measure, report and have verified their forest results and claim results-based payments from donors (the rbf branch): training and data collection with 15 countries in 2024 (forest reference levels, greenhouse-gas inventories, biennial reports; the forestry experts' $631,375 in Schedule O) and the negotiations on REDD+ finance. A tenth goes to the climate-finance goal (fin_share_of_programme). The rest goes to the carbon markets of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (the itmo branch): negotiating its rules, completed at COP29 in 2024, and national implementation in four countries (carbon-market laws, registries, readying Suriname's credits for sale), which the 2024 Impact Statement gives as much space. Anchor: the statement's own weight among its pillars; travel and meetings ($522,448) serve all three.

rows.label: Share of the programme on the negotiations for the climate-finance goal
rows.explainer: The finance goal was one of the two COP29 results CfRN's Impact Statement leads with, but one strand of its negotiations work beside REDD+ and Article 6, which take its data, legal and implementation teams. Our judgment a tenth (3-20%) of the programme.

Climate-finance goal: CfRN's spending on it in 2024

Climate-finance goal agreed at COP29: a year by 2035

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: all countries had agreed to triple climate finance for developing countries from $100 to $300 billion annually by 2035

rows.explainer: The new collective quantified goal: developed countries to provide or mobilise $300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035.

rows.label: The $100 billion goal it replaces

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: all countries had agreed to triple climate finance for developing countries from $100 to $300 billion annually by 2035

rows.explainer: The goal set in 2009 for 2020, which the new goal triples.

rows.label: Share of the rise in climate finance that the goal itself causes
rows.explainer: Climate finance was rising before the goal and would go on rising with development banks' plans and donors' budgets; a goal adds pressure and a yardstick, but nothing binds a donor (the US left the Paris Agreement in 2025, and the $100 billion goal was reached late). Our judgment: 15% of the $200 billion rise is the goal's own doing (3-40%). Whether it is delivered at all is fin_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Share of the goal's finance worth as much as a grant
rows.explainer: The goal counts loans at face value and private money mobilised; a loan repaid is worth only its subsidy to the borrower. Our judgment 40% (20-70%), the grant-equivalent part.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of a grant-equivalent dollar of aid
rows.explainer: Aid won whose use isn't modelled is valued at the site's shared figure for a donor's aid budget (docs/normalization.md 2.20): climate finance funds adaptation, energy and other development projects much like other aid.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of the finance it adds a year, once in effect
REDD+ results-based payments committed by climate funds and donors, 2010-2021

source.title: Forest Declaration Assessment (February 2022), Reward results by countries and jurisdictions
source.quote: Just over USD 6.7 billion has been committed by multilateral climate funds and bilateral donors through REDD+, of which USD 4.6 billion went to results-based payments

rows.explainer: Every results-based payment for reduced deforestation committed since 2010 (Norway, Germany, the Green Climate Fund, the World Bank's Carbon Fund and others), in every REDD+ country, not only those CfRN works with: the attribution row below sets CfRN's spending against all the resources in the same countries, so the countries' share cancels (it would scale the tonnes and the resources alike).

rows.label: REDD+ readiness and implementation finance committed, 2010-2021

source.title: Forest Declaration Assessment (February 2022), Reward results by countries and jurisdictions
source.quote: the remaining USD 1.8 billion to readiness and implementation

rows.explainer: Grants for the kind of work CfRN does: helping countries build forest monitoring, reference levels and REDD+ strategies.

rows.label: Forest countries' own REDD+ spending committed, 2010-2021

source.title: Forest Declaration Assessment (February 2022), Reward results by countries and jurisdictions
source.quote: USD 10.1 billion has been committed by forest country governments for activities under their REDD+ plans

rows.explainer: The forest countries' own budgets for their REDD+ plans: enforcement, land-use planning and forest agencies, the work that actually keeps forest standing. The assessment notes it is unclear how much was spent.

rows.label: Years the assessment's totals cover

source.title: Forest Declaration Assessment (February 2022), Reward results by countries and jurisdictions
source.quote: Since 2010, approximately USD 24.5 billion – an average of USD 2.4 billion per year – has been channeled

rows.explainer: The assessment's own average: $24.5 billion at $2.4 billion a year is about ten years, 2010 to about 2020 (published February 2022). It cancels out of the result (rbp_per_year scales the tonnes and CfRN's share alike).

rows.label: Results-based payments a year, all REDD+ countries
rows.explainer: About $460 million a year. Commitments, not disbursements: some is paid years later or never (the shortfall sits in rbp_evidence_adj; the attribution row divides by commitments too).

rows.label: Forest countries' REDD+ spending as a share of their commitments, against donors'
rows.explainer: The assessment warns that it is "unclear to what extent" the forest countries' $10.1 billion was spent (p. 3), and that less than half of the climate funds' REDD+ pledges had been disbursed (p. 6). Donors' commitments and the countries' are both counted as committed, so what matters is whether the countries spent a smaller share of theirs than donors did. Our judgment: about the same (1), from half to one and a half times.

rows.label: All REDD+ resources per dollar of results-based payments
rows.explainer: Payments, readiness grants and the forest countries' own budgets over payments, about 3.6: for each dollar paid for results, about $2.60 more of others' money works on the same forests. Used for both forest branches: the governments selling credits under Article 6 run the same REDD+ programmes, with the same readiness support.

rows.label: Carbon markets: money paid a year for rainforest countries' forest credits under Article 6, once the market works
rows.explainer: No forest credit had been transferred under Article 6 by the end of 2024: Suriname announced the world's first sale of such credits (Impact Statement 2024, p. 4) and expected it in 2025. Anchors: Hess's purchase of Guyana's jurisdictional credits, at least $750 million over 2022-2032, about $75 million a year for one country; all donors' results-based payments, about $460 million a year. Our judgment: $200 million a year ($50 million to $1 billion). It cancels out of the result: CfRN's share of the resources falls as the market grows (itmo_attribution_share).

rows.label: Carbon markets: price of a forest credit (a tonne of reduced emissions)

source.title: Stabroek News (11 January 2023), Hess makes US$75M first payment for Guyana-issued carbon credits
source.quote: US$37.5 million for 2.5 million ART-TREES credits from 2016 at a price of US$15/tonne of CO2e

rows.explainer: Hess's deal with Guyana, the largest sale of a country's forest credits so far, is worth at least $750 million between 2022 and 2032; its first payment priced the 2016 and 2017 credits at $15 a tonne, and later vintages are priced higher (Hess's announcement gives 37.5 million credits for the $750 million, $20 on average). Our estimate $20 ($10-30): $10 is the low end of jurisdictional forest credits, $30 a price only the best-rated units reach.

rows.label: Carbon markets: forest credits sold a year
Tropical forest in the countries working under the UN's REDD+ framework

source.title: Coalition for Rainforest Nations, Annual Impact Statement 2024
source.quote: around 90% of the world’s tropical forests and span an area of about 1.6 billion hectares

rows.explainer: Context only, not on the path to the result: the forest the payments and credit sales below can reward (read by tco2e_per_hectare_year): the model counts tonnes from dollars, not from hectares, because neither CfRN nor its partner countries publish the forest their finance keeps. The hectares kept a year are rbf_ha_per_year and itmo_ha_per_year.

rows.label: Health: people with fewer illnesses from the forest kept
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Livelihoods: people whose income changes
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Wellbeing: people whose life satisfaction rises from nature kept
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: animal-years affected
rows.explainer: Not counted: CfRN works with governments on national forest accounting and finance, and neither it nor its partner countries report effects on health, incomes, recreation or wild animals that could be traced to that work. 0.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, Guyana 2010-2015 (dollars of the time)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: Based on assumed payments of US$250 million, the cost of the 12.8 million tons of avoided CO2 emissions is US$19.53 per ton of CO2.

rows.explainer: The one quasi-experimental evaluation of a national results-based REDD+ programme: Norway's offer of $250 million to Guyana for keeping deforestation low in 2010-2015 cut tree-cover loss by 35% against a synthetic control, 12.8 million tonnes of CO₂, $19.53 a tonne if the loss avoided is permanent (that question is permanence_share). The paper reports bootstrapped 95% intervals only in its appendix; the range, $12 to $40, is ours, wider on the high side because Guyana's reference level was set high and other countries' programmes may buy less.

rows.label: Years of the Norway-Guyana payments (2010-2015)

source.title: Roopsind, Sohngen and Brandt (2019), Evidence that a national REDD+ program reduces tree cover loss and carbon emissions in a high forest cover, low deforestation country, PNAS 116(49): 24492-24499
source.quote: with Norway offering to pay US$250 million to Guyana if annual deforestation rates remained below 0.056% from 2010 to 2015.

rows.explainer: Six years, 2010 to 2015: the payments' price level is the average of those years'.

rows.label: Results-based payments per tonne of CO₂ kept out of the air, in 2024 dollars
rows.explainer: Guyana's cost per tonne in 2024 prices (× US consumer prices in 2024 over their 2010-2015 average, about 1.36: Convention 8), so that it divides 2024 dollars of payments, credit sales and CfRN's spending alike: about $26.65.

rows.label: Share of the forest kept that stays standing for good
rows.explainer: Tree-cover loss in Guyana rose after the payments ended (Roopsind et al. 2019: "without continued payments, forest protection is not guaranteed"), so some forest kept is only cleared later. Our judgment half (20-90%), as for the site's other forest models (Rainforest Foundation US, Cool Earth).

rows.label: Share of the clearing avoided that moves elsewhere
rows.explainer: A country paid to clear less may push clearing (gold mining, farming, logging) across the border; Roopsind et al. flag leakage as possible but unmeasured. Our judgment 20% (0-50%), as for the leakage rows of The Nature Conservancy's forest branches. Failure of the main effect, so it stays in the main chain, not among side effects.

rows.label: How far Guyana's result holds for the payments CfRN's countries get
rows.explainer: Guyana's is one country, with low deforestation and a forward-looking contract that rewarded each year's restraint. Most of the money CfRN helps countries claim pays for results years after the fact (Honduras's 2016-2020 results were verified in 2024), which rewards the past more than it changes the future, and reference levels set high pay for reductions that would have come anyway. Our judgment 0.5 (0.2-1), anchored on The Nature Conservancy's 0.4-0.75 for forest rules judged from other places' studies. Used for both branches' forest tonnes.

rows.label: CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost
rows.explainer: The tropics' average, 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares lost in 2023 (about 650 tonnes a hectare; World Resources Institute, the shared figures every forest model reads). Only used to turn tonnes into hectares for the pandemic-risk rows.

rows.label: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all the finance, per hectare of REDD+ forest
rows.explainer: For reading only: the forest carbon the donors' payments and the credit sales keep a year (before CfRN's share), spread over the 1.6 billion hectares under REDD+. Nothing on the path reads it.

rows.label: Years of forest kept that a year's work counts
rows.explainer: One, for the two forest branches (the finance goal counts its own won years, fin_years): both set a year of CfRN's spending against a year of the finance flows it shares in, with CfRN credited its share of that year's resources (an ongoing flow counts one year against one year's cost, Convention 3). The new Article 6 rules are part of the stock of rules and institutions every year's flow rests on, which is why the flow, not the rule, is counted.

rows.label: Years from the year's work until the forest is kept
rows.explainer: Countries CfRN helps report in one year and are paid a year or more later (Honduras's results verified in 2024, its first sales planned for 2025); Article 6's first forest credits were due on the market in 2025-2027. The forest kept follows the expectation of payment, so about two years (half a year to four). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years of forest kept, discounted
Results-based finance: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by all donors' payments, for good
rows.explainer: The year's payments over the cost per tonne, × the share that stays standing, × the share not displaced. How far Guyana's result holds is the branch's evidence adjustment.

rows.label: Results-based finance: CO₂ kept, discounted years
Results-based finance: tropical forest kept a year
Carbon markets: CO₂ kept out of the air a year by the money buyers pay
rows.explainer: The same chain as results-based payments: money paid for results keeps forest standing at Guyana's cost per tonne, × permanence, × leakage, × how far Guyana's result holds (applied here, not in the branch's evidence row, so it doesn't shrink the buyers' extra emissions below as well).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of the credits bought by countries for their own targets
rows.explainer: Article 6 credits go to countries counting them against their national pledges (Switzerland, Sweden, Japan, Singapore's government), to airlines under CORSIA, to companies under carbon taxes that accept them (Singapore's), and to companies buying voluntarily (CfRN's REDD.plus platform). CfRN's own plan is purchases "by corporations and sovereign governments", possibly through a carbon tax like Singapore's (Impact Statement 2024, p. 32). Our judgment: half to countries (20-80%).

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of countries' credits that replace cuts they would otherwise make
rows.explainer: A country that counts a forest credit against its own target can cut a tonne less at home. If the credit is a real extra tonne kept, the two cancel; if not, the world emits more. The real tonnes are itmo_forest_tco2e_per_year; this row is how many of countries' credits replace cuts they would otherwise have made. A country that would have met its target anyway replaces cuts one for one; one that would have missed it (CfRN: the credits "help developed countries who fail to hit their climate pledges") replaces fewer. Our judgment half (20-90%). The failure of the market's main chain (credits for reductions that would have happened anyway), so it is in the main chain, not a side effect.

rows.label: Carbon markets: real cuts in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought

source.title: Probst et al. (2024), Systematic assessment of the achieved emission reductions of carbon crediting projects, Nature Communications
source.quote: We estimate that less than 16% of the carbon credits issued to the investigated projects constitute real emission reductions

rows.explainer: An airline under CORSIA or a company buying voluntarily would otherwise have bought another credit; a company under a carbon tax would otherwise have paid the tax. So a forest credit they buy instead loses only the real cut in the unit it displaced, and none where the tax would have been paid. Probst et al. (2024) find under 16% of credits issued are real cuts (25% for avoided deforestation). 16% (0-40%), no fuel smoke: the displaced units are mostly other offsets.

rows.label: Carbon markets: extra fossil emissions by country buyers a year
Carbon markets: extra emissions a year from all buyers
rows.explainer: Countries' forgone cuts at home, plus the real cuts lost in the units other buyers would otherwise have bought.

rows.label: Carbon markets: CO₂ kept a year, net of buyers' extra emissions
rows.explainer: Negative when the buyers' extra emissions exceed the real tonnes the money keeps: at the best guesses each credit sold at $20 keeps about a fifth of a tonne of forest carbon (Probst et al. 2024 find a quarter of avoided-deforestation credits real, a cross-check) and lets buyers emit about a third of a tonne more.

rows.label: Carbon markets: net CO₂, discounted years
Carbon markets: tropical forest kept a year
Catastrophic risk: deaths if the catastrophe happens
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance below is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about 2% a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drove
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than 30% of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (facts/catastrophe.json, as for The Nature Conservancy): half of the land-use risk scales with tropical forest loss (10-100%), anchored on Allen et al. (2017). No study has measured this dose.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance per hectare of tropical forest kept
rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept, as in the site's other forest model. The least grounded number here.

rows.label: Results-based finance: fall in the yearly pandemic chance × discounted years
Carbon markets: fall in the yearly pandemic chance × discounted years
rows.explainer: From the forest kept only; the buyers' extra emissions clear no forest.

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: mostly older people died, few young children.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: school-age children were the least affected.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: about 15% of adult excess deaths were under 50; the rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number.

rows.label: Results-based finance: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value
Carbon markets: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value
Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance from the year's work
rows.explainer: For reading: the forest each branch keeps × its credit × the risk per hectare.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: share of the win due to all its advocates
rows.explainer: The goal is agreed, so the chance is the shared share of a won climate policy due to all advocates together, rather than to governments, events and opinion (facts/climate.json, 30%, 10-60%); CfRN's part of the advocates is fin_attribution_share.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years of negotiation behind it
rows.explainer: The talks on the new goal ran from the decision at COP26 (2021) to its adoption at COP29 (2024), about three years (2-5). As a past average, a year's spending gets one year's share of the win (Convention 11).

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: years until the added finance flows, on average
rows.explainer: The goal is for 2035, eleven years after it was agreed; finance rises towards it, so the added money comes on average about six years after the year's work (3-11). Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The site's years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted, normalization.md 2.9), after the wait, discounted.

rows.label: Climate-finance goal: value of the finance added, one year's share of the win
rows.explainer: The value of the finance the goal adds a year × the advocates' share of the win × the discounted years counted ÷ the years of negotiation. Compliance costs (normalization.md 2.21): none counted, since the goal binds no payer and each dollar given is valued as aid, the donors' cost being the site's convention for aid won.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: The shared judgment: 0, the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above.

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future generations' healthy years
rows.explainer: 0 at the best guess (future_share_lost); credited by branch.

rows.label: Health: DALYs averted per person per year
rows.explainer: Not reached: the matching reach row is 0.

rows.label: Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per person per year
rows.explainer: Not reached: the matching reach row is 0.

rows.label: Wellbeing: life satisfaction gained per person per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Not reached: the matching reach row is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of disabling pain spared per animal-year
rows.explainer: Not reached: the matching reach row is 0.

rows.label: Results-based finance: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: How far Guyana's result holds for the payments CfRN's countries get (the row it reads).

rows.label: Results-based finance: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the cost per tonne is from a comparison with a synthetic control, so the forest that would have stood anyway is already out of it; whether the money would have reached the countries without CfRN is its share of the resources (one question per adjustment).

rows.label: Results-based finance: CfRN's share of the resources behind the forest kept
rows.explainer: CfRN's spending on this branch over every REDD+ resource a year: the donors' payments, readiness grants and the forest countries' own budgets (Convention 2). About 0.15%: the payers and the governments that do the protecting are almost all of it. Measured over all REDD+ countries, which scales the tonnes alike.

rows.label: Results-based finance: delivery
rows.explainer: 1: money committed but not paid lowers the payments and the resources alike, and payments for old results are in the evidence row.

rows.label: Results-based finance: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: Thin: neither CfRN nor its countries measure the forest its work keeps; the branch rests on one evaluation in Guyana and judgment (Convention 12).

rows.label: Results-based finance: adjustments that read no shared value
rows.explainer: Split out so the share of fossil tonnes (fuel_share) can be weighted by branch without reading a shared value; the missing-data discount and next-dollar factor are the same for both forest branches.

rows.label: Results-based finance: all adjustments
Results-based finance: credit
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × the next-dollar factor: the share of resources is an average over everyone's past spending (estimate_basis past_average).

rows.label: Carbon markets: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 1 here: how far Guyana's result holds is applied to the forest tonnes only (itmo_forest_tco2e_per_year), so it doesn't also shrink the buyers' extra emissions.

rows.label: Carbon markets: share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: as for results-based finance; whether the market would work without CfRN is its share of the resources.

rows.explainer: CfRN's spending on Article 6 negotiations and national implementation over all the resources behind the forest credits sold a year: the buyers' payments, the sellers' REDD+ programmes and readiness support, in the same proportion as for donors' payments (redd_resources_per_rbp_dollar). About 0.3% at the best guesses. CfRN is one of many negotiating parties and groups on Article 6, so its share of the rules is small too; that is inside this share of all the market's resources.

Our judgment 0.05% (0.01-0.3%), about CfRN's spending on the talks over a few hundred million dollars a year of everyone's. Anchor: the site's other models of large multilateral wins credit a single group well under 1%.

rows.explainer: Nothing binds a donor to the goal; the largest, the US, left the Paris Agreement in 2025, and aid budgets in Europe are being cut. Our judgment half (20-90%).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: the payers' money is already in each branch's share of the resources. Below 1 if CfRN's funders would otherwise fund similar REDD+ support; above 1 if its help brings in money that wouldn't go to forests at all. Range 0.85-1.1. Applied to all branches.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the result
rows.explainer: Positive: the integrity rules CfRN pressed for in Article 6 (reviews that flag inconsistent credits), and greenhouse-gas inventories that countries also use for their national climate pledges. Negative: donors may shift money from results-based grants to buying credits they count against their own targets. Net 0 (−20% to +20%). Applied to the whole result, harms included.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: 0: forest carbon is CO₂, and the buyers' extra emissions are counted as CO₂ too.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: Forest carbon carries no fuel smoke; the buyers' extra emissions do, and they are negative tonnes in the total. So this is the buyers' credited tonnes over the net credited tonnes, negative (or above 1 when the net is negative), so that air pollution counts for the buyers' tonnes alone. Weighted by tonnes a year with each branch's adjustments that read no shared value; both forest branches share the same years, wait, missing-data discount and next-dollar factor, which cancel, so the weighting is exact (the finance branch has no tonnes).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of the buyers' fuel, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Buyers of forest credits are rich countries (Switzerland, Singapore, Japan, Sweden) and airlines under CORSIA, whose forgone cuts are in power plants with scrubbers, vehicles and jet fuel burnt mostly at altitude. Anchors: the site's shared factors for US power (0.013), US vehicles (0.04) and California's cap-and-invest (0.07); jet fuel at altitude adds little ground-level smoke. Our judgment 0.025 (0.01-0.14).

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes carry, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).
